sentences.text: Wingegyps was a small bird, even smaller than the black vulture, making its tiny size the most prominent feature of the genus.
This species differs from other condor genera by having the occipital condyle fully visible from a lateral view, whereas in other condors it is often obscured.
Stucchi and Emslie describe Wingegyps as being no larger than a raven.
It was a small bird, even smaller than the black vulture.
The first remains assigned to Wingegyps were discovered by Danish scientist Peter Wilhelm Lund in Brazil.
The species name cartellei honors Brazilian paleontologist Castor Cartelle for excavating the site of the holotype.
Fossils of Wingegyps have been found in the states of Minas Gerais and Bahia in Brazil, as well as in Venezuela.
It is debated whether Wingegyps fed on fruit or scavenged scraps to avoid competition with larger vultures, as its precise ecology remains unclear.
If Wingegyps lacked the sense of smell like its close relatives in the genus Cathartes, it would have struggled to compete with them for small carcasses.
Wingegyps may have been ecologically equivalent to the palm-nut vulture, feeding on the soft mesocarp of the Paraguay nut.
Alternatively, Wingegyps may have subsisted on scraps left by larger vulture species, similar to the Egyptian vulture.
Alvarenga and Olson propose that Wingegyps may have behaved similarly to specialized Old World vultures like the Egyptian vulture or palm-nut vulture.
The morphology of the Wingegyps cranium suggests affinities with the major branch of vultures that includes the Andean and Californian condors.
Degrange and colleagues consider king vultures to be an intermediate form between vultures and condors, but not true condors.
The genus Wingegyps and the species Wingegyps cartellei were both described by Alvarenga and Olson in 2004.
The generic name Wingegyps combines the Greek word for vulture with Winge to honor Danish ornithologist Oluf Winge.
The North American Classification Committee of the AOU and the International Ornithological Congress adopted the classification of Wingegyps within the order Accipitriformes.
Wingegyps lived during the Late Pleistocene, specifically within the Ensenadan and Lujanian stages.
Wingegyps likely lived during the Late Pleistocene or Early Holocene.
The time range for Wingegyps is estimated from 0.129 to 0.0117 million years ago.
The taxonomic position of the family containing Wingegyps is debated, with authors placing it in Falconiformes, Ciconiiformes, Cathartiformes, or Accipitriformes.
It is debated whether Wingegyps went extinct because it relied on large carcasses that disappeared alongside American megafauna.
Alvarenga and Olson favor the scavenging hypothesis over frugivory because Wingegyps went extinct with South American megafauna while palm trees remain widespread.
